newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hillary Clinton urges respect for womens' roles.
newsitem.headline: Hillary Clinton urges respect for womens' roles.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Tuesday urged a greater recognition of the role of women in promoting prosperity and upholding democracy and called for increased community aid investment.

Addressing a 600-strong, predominantly female audience of dignitaries, aid workers and academics, Rodham Clinton said that the worst excesses of inhumanity occurred in countries which had lost sight of what women held most dear -- the care and nurture of children and families.
"If women were to stop working tomorrow inside and outside the home, the economy would collapse in short order," she told the gathering at the University of Amsterdam.

"The future of democracy depends not solely on our concept of realpolitik between and among nations, but what I have come to call real life politics -- in other words...it is about the internalisation of democratic values in people's minds and hearts," Rodham Clinton said.

Echoing George Marshall, U.S. architect of Europe's post-war reconstruction, she added: "Democratic principles do not flourish on empty stomachs...social investments are as critical to democracy and prosperity as free markets and trade."

America's First Lady arrived at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport early on Tuesday for a programme of solo engagements before joining President Bill Clinton when he arrives in the Hague for meetings on Wednesday with the European Union.

The visit is combined with a commemoration of the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Aid Plan, which will be attended by leaders from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which groups Europe, Canada and the United States.

Rodham Clinton's tour of the Dutch capital takes in its most well-known sights, including a boat trip through the canals, a visit to the Rijksmuseum and a visit to the canal-side refuge of Jewish teenage wartime diarist Anne Frank.
"It's the classic first-time tour of Amsterdam," said one Washington aide.

A first for Rodham Clinton, the visit is also the first of its kind since 1788 when Abigail Adams, wife of future president John Adams, accompanied her husband and Thomas Jefferson to Amsterdam to raise funds from Dutch bankers for the fledgling U.S. congress.
